name: Pareto Principle
description: A common rule of thumb that a minority of causes often drives a majority of outcomes, popularly phrased as 80/20. In UX practice it is used to justify prioritizing the few features, issues, or user paths thought to matter most.
design_relevance_note: Common in research synthesis, backlog triage, analytics review, and prioritization conversations about which problems or features deserve the most design effort.
myth_risk_note: No empirical validation of the Pareto principle as a design law specific to UX/HCI was found. The principle is cited in economics and business contexts but lacks the kind of controlled, replicable user-centered evidence that would establish it as a robust design heuristic. Consistent with this entry's existing no_rigorous_backing_found status.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and common in product/UX prioritization discussions, analytics triage, and issue-ranking practice, though usually as a planning heuristic rather than an interaction-design law.

applications.title: Hypothetical: prioritizing 3 features responsible for 86% of negative feedback
applications.description: NN/g's own worked example for applying the Pareto Principle to UX prioritization: an app's customer-satisfaction rating is declining, so the team runs a Pareto analysis on negative feedback by product feature and finds that just 3 features account for 86% of all negative submissions -- used to argue for concentrating fix effort on those 3 features ahead of other, easier-to-fix features with less impact.
applications.ethical_note: Directing limited UX resources toward the features causing the most user-reported pain is a straightforwardly user-beneficial use of prioritization data, with no persuasion or dark-pattern dimension. The real risk region for Pareto-style prioritization, per the source's own 'Dangers of Focusing on ONLY 20%' section, is neglecting the remaining 80% of the experience over time -- a resourcing tradeoff, not a manipulation of users.
